The open items of Spinbox's security model, from spin's [`docs/security/README.md`](https://github.com/spin-stack/spin/blob/3cb9bb55ff21e9b9ff669480dc9053aa9dee732a/docs/security/README.md) at `3cb9bb55f`. The numbers are [its rules](/reference/security/rules/).

What no line keeps yet. Each is a design change, not a patch, which is why it is here.

- **A team's network policy reaches what its admins say.** Where an installation sets
  `team_network_policies`, any team's admin - and every person administers their personal team -
  can let that team's workspaces reach any destination past the node drops, whatever the
  installation's own policies allow. The setting is the whole control; there is no ceiling a
  team's policy is held under.
- **I12 through a proxy holds as the proxy does.** The proxy is asked to connect to the address
  that was checked, and one that connects elsewhere is the operator's choice, as the proxy is. The
  storage endpoint an admin sets is deliberately exempt: an S3 inside the installation's own
  network is the normal deployment.
- **A name a policy allows is held to what DNS and the client say.** An address serving many names
  is open to all of them once one is allowed; a rule that checks SNI (`netpolicy.Rule.VerifySNI`)
  narrows that for a client that names the host it wants, and passes a tenant that names an allowed
  host to reach another behind the same address (domain fronting). Only a brokered rule that
  injects, whose proxy holds each request's `Host` to the name, keeps a tenant to it. The resolver
  takes upstream only what a policy names (`network.Fabric.asks`), so a name is a channel only to
  whoever answers one a policy allows: a wildcard over a domain that strangers can publish under is
  a way out, by its questions as by its addresses.
- **Every host writes `layers/`.** A layer is content-addressed, create-only and locked, and opened
  only through a manifest its writer signed, so a host can add layers nothing reads - and pay for
  them - and change none. Under the volumes it writes only its own subtree of each, never the
  grant or the descriptor (`bucketpolicy.For`), and nothing there is served without its holder's
  signature and grant. A host a volume left keeps that credential for up to a quarter of an hour,
  which the store cannot end early: it reads the volume as it held it - and a snapshot asked for
  before the move, which the new holder seals under the version it was asked at - and adds commits
  and HEADs under its own subtree that no restore takes, each counted as it is passed over and every
  request in the bucket's access log (I8).
- **A key a host was given opens what it sealed until the volume is re-keyed.** A volume's key
  never turns, and an honest host forgets it when the volume leaves; one running other code keeps it. Revoking
  a host marks every volume it was granted for a re-key, which runs once the workspace is stopped:
  until then the layers that key opens are open to whoever holds it, and the re-key deletes the
  volume's snapshots with it, being exactly what that key opens.
- **A move between a detach and its attach is the old host's.** A grant is made over the HEAD the
  volume's history reaches when the control plane places it, so what the host it left wrote in
  that window - seconds, when the move is one `RecoverWorkspace` - is history the new holder starts
  from.
- **I14 and I15 in a development installation.** A developer's runner is not root: its QEMU and
  its qemu-img run as itself, with nothing of root's to keep from them, and a kernel without
  core scheduling runs machines side by side on one core's siblings. Such an installation places
  on any host; only a production one requires what each host says it keeps.
- **What a host says it keeps is the host's word.** On AWS that is the word of a runner build
  the host proved it booted (I13), on the image whose kernel has all three; a self-hosted host's
  is believed as its registration token is.
- **I16 tells a store's clients apart by port, not by what each asks.** Neither Quickwit nor the
  metric store's writes take a key, so the kernel refuses a connection by the caller's group, and
  a client let through a port has all of it: the collector reaches the whole of Quickwit's gRPC,
  which carries Quickwit's own services beside the logs it is sent, and Grafana can write samples
  as well as read them. Root on the control plane's machine can drop the table; that root is the
  installation already.
- **Which release of the CLI a person runs.** A CLI behind its installation replaces itself with
  the release the control plane names (`internal/selfupdate`), and `spin update` does so for any
  release it names, an older one included. Only what the release workflow signed and attested of
  that very version is installed, checked offline before it replaces anything, so a control plane
  cannot have a CLI run a binary of its own. It can have `spin update` install an older signed one,
  with whatever that one got wrong; the automatic update only ever moves forward.
- **A workspace's owner sees who opens its pages.** Signing in to a workspace's host gives that host a
  session for that workspace alone, which the API refuses, and a page on the host can read how it got
  there. So its owner can act as the visitor on their own workspace and nowhere else, and learns
  that the person visited.
- **Workspaces are one site to a browser unless `ws.<domain>` is on the public suffix list.** A
  dashboard cookie is host-only and the API refuses it from another origin, and the proxy asks as
  nobody for another workspace's page, by `Origin`, `Sec-Fetch-Site` and `Referer`. A link followed
  from another workspace still carries the visitor's session on the workspace it opens, as a top-level
  navigation has to: `SameSite=Lax` sends it on a link from any site, so that listing does not change
  it. What the listing does change is what a tenant's page can do with cookies of its own: until
  then it can set one with `Domain=<domain>`, or `Domain=ws.<domain>`, which reaches the dashboard's
  host and every other workspace. A browser that sends no `Sec-Fetch-Site` is not told apart from a tool on a plain `GET`. Sessions issued
  through a workspace before this release can reach the whole account until they expire.
- **I17 and I18 hold against an operator, not against the tenant, nor a guest.** Root in a guest is anybody the access lets in - its owner and each guest alike: it can
  rewrite the drop-in and the supervisor's answers. Sealing keeps everyone else out; it does not
  keep the people let in from the machine they were let into.
- **A browser session logs in for 7 days, and changes an access, with nobody asked.** Code running on
  the terminal's origin - already trusted with every signature there - or malware in the browser uses
  its session key without a prompt until the grant ends; ending the session (`#/session`) drops the
  key, and taking the passkey that signed it out of the keyring ends the grant at every host within
  `roster.Fresh`. Past the first, the key also signs any access that lets nobody new in - guests
  taken out - by a click at most, and none of it ends with the grant. It signs no settings: those
  take a key of the keyring (I18). A host reads an
  access for the workspace's life, and a word's own date is the key's to write, so holding it to
  the grant is only the control plane's, when it keeps it (`SetOwnerWord`): a taken one keeps what
  such code signs after the grant ended, and it stands while the passkey stays in the keyring. The
  key stays in the browser until the session ends. What a host holds a session key's access to is the people it names, against the
  word below it (`ownerword.highest`), so no script or control plane lets anybody in with it.
  A first access the key signed is read for the workspace's life, held only to having been taken
  while the grant held (`SetOwnerWord`). The control plane holds no key that signs one, but it
  serves the page that frames the agent's: while a grant holds and the dashboard is open, it can
  make a workspace in the person's name and frame it, and the session key signs that first access
  with no prompt and nothing on screen. It gets a word naming the image and team it chose, so
  identity tokens naming the person for a disk it chose, for any audience the installation allows;
  it gets no login, guests or settings (`ownerword.Word.Minimal`, I18) and none of the workspaces
  that have a word. A link to a terminal of its own got the same for one click, so this was accepted. A script
  on the dashboard's origin reaches the same, for an image the installation allows.
- **Taking a passkey out of a keyring locks what it signed.** A workspace whose newest access that
  passkey or its session key signed lets nobody in until its owner signs it again with another key,
  one signature per workspace. It is the only remote revocation for a stolen laptop, and most
  workspaces hang on one passkey, so the page leads its owner to that signature (`enter`). An owner
  whose keyring started anew cannot sign one, and recovers the workspace instead.
- **A person's first keyring is whoever signs it first.** A keyring's first version is taken as it
  is signed: nothing names a person's keys before it. A stolen account, or a control plane running someone else's code,
  can sign one for somebody who has not yet, list the person's passkey beside its own when they
  register one, and log in to all they make. It holds for anybody whose first keyring was signed
  before: the chain is then theirs.
- **A synced passkey is as safe as what syncs it.** Whoever gets into a person's Apple or Google
  account, or their password manager, holds their passkey and signs as them: the same as the person
  to every host. It is a third party outside the control plane and the operator, accepted so that a
  person has one passkey rather than one per browser. A security key stays on the device.
- **What is typed in an overlaid Agent frame reaches T3 Code.** The dashboard frames the agent's page
  and can lay words over it, as it cannot over the routes that sign: typing goes to the client, as
  the agent's user. A terminal stays in a tab of its own for this reason, a shell there being root.
- **A guest is let into the guest by the same certificate as the owner.** The host decides who
  logs in, not what a login may do: a guest is root, and changes nothing the control plane holds -
  `middleware.guestMay` - but can change the machine itself. Sharing a workspace is trusting the
  guest with it.
- **A person's agent CLI credentials are one, for all their workspaces.** Claude Code's and Codex's
  credentials files are kept as the person's (`agent_credentials`, sealed) and handed to every
  workspace they own, so one login signs in each (`supervisorserver.pushCredentials`,
  `agentcredentials.Keeper`). So whoever runs code in one of them - the agent itself, led there by
  what it read, or a dependency the workspace installed - holds the provider token of every one, and
  a change it sends replaces the copy they all use, until the person logs out or revokes it at the
  provider. Only a workspace its owner's alone is handed any or has one taken from it
  (`workspaces.owners_alone`, `supervisorserver.holdsCredentials`): made of an image, of a
  snapshot or clone of a workspace of theirs that is so too, or of the prebuild of a project they
  may open, mounting an agent's home only such workspaces mounted (`agent_volumes.owners_alone`),
  never naming a guest, and never a prebuild's build. A prebuild's disk holds what the
  repository's code did in its build, which is no more than that code does as root in a workspace
  opened straight from the repository; the build, which nobody watches and every member opens, is
  handed nothing. A copy of another person's snapshot, and every workspace and home made before
  the mark was kept, get none, and the person signs in there as before. Its
  supervisor takes out what it held once the access names a guest (`handler.TakeOwnerWord`). What
  does not leave with the files: a guest named while the agent was signed in may read what the
  machine kept of them - freed blocks of the agent's home, and the memory of a CLI the agent's
  stopped server did not end.
- **A guest trusts the egress root its control plane hands it.** Every registration hands the
  installation's root, and the guest puts it in its trust store (`handler.InstallEgressCA`): a root
  there reads what the guest's TLS clients send through a proxy that holds it. Only the egress proxy
  of the host the workspace runs on is issued under it, and that host is one the control plane can
  open a root shell on anyway; nothing an owner says narrows it.
- **Logs leave as the installation says.** A guest's journal and a machine's console are collected
  while the installation's policy collects them (`LogCollection`, `HostPolicy.collect_console`),
  and the agent's thread index is reported always: titles, paths and times, never a message. An owner
  has no say over it, so an installation admin's session - stolen or not - reads every collected
  journal: a decision, not an oversight.
- **A key taken out of a keyring works for up to `roster.Fresh` (5 minutes) more.** A host reads a
  keyring again when what it holds is older than that, so a key taken out still logs in, and settings
  it signed still apply, at a host that read the keyring just before.
- **A repository approval is not withdrawn.** Settings name each repository a workspace of the person
  opened, and signing new settings is the only way to drop one: nothing takes an approval back
  without the person's key, and nothing reminds them that one stands.
- **The terminal's code is trusted as the proxy serves it.** `term.<domain>`, and the agent's
  client it frames at `agents.<domain>`, are the release's signed files on the proxy image's verity
  root, under a Caddyfile spin-boot carries, so the control plane changes neither; a
  proxy running other code serves any code that holds a session and asks the passkey.
- **The published key set is the identity key's first version, as the proxy serves it.**
  `id.<domain>` is written on the proxy from the first version of `identity/issuer.json` and its CA,
  which no role may delete, so another key the control plane writes publishes
  nothing; a proxy running other code publishes any key set. A self-hosted installation
  serves none.
- **I19 holds the identity key to the image a host booted, not to the host.** Every host shares
  the key, because the published key set is one key: a runner running other code signs for any
  subject. A self-hosted installation has no key service, and its control plane keeps the key it
  grants.
- **A keyring and a roster are trusted from their first version.** A version is signed by a key
  the one before trusts, and kept under the bucket's lock in GOVERNANCE, which the account's root
  can lift. A user or a team made by a control plane running someone else's code starts a chain whose first
  version the control plane can sign - and a team it makes is its own, which nothing trusts. A version
  already kept is not written over: on AWS the bucket's policy refuses a write under `rosters/`
  without `If-None-Match`. A store with no such policy has only the client's word for it.

## What this does not protect

The control plane holds what it needs to serve people. What follows is what it could do with that if
someone ran their own code with its permissions. This is an assumption the design is checked against,
not a finding: no way of doing that is known, and no outside test has looked for one yet. Below, "it"
is such a control plane.

- **The storage layer holds nothing against it.** The control plane mints every credential and
  grants every key, so it could clone any snapshot to a workspace of its own on an attested runner,
  and come in with a keyring of its own.
- **I17, I18 and I19 do not hold against a control plane that uses a host.** It can open a root shell
  on any host (`OpenHostShellCommand`): both keys are its own, and the host checks only the time and
  the keys' shape. Emptying the host first, the approval and the recording are the control plane's
  own code, which other code would skip. Root on a host reads and writes every workspace on it,
  memory included, and is answered by the key service as that host is. Holding the shell to a key
  the control plane does not have is not built: a lost key would leave a host with no way in during
  an incident, and it would only narrow what is described here (`CLAUDE.md`).
- **The owner's word names no disk.** A host takes the spec's volume over the one it held, since a
  restore changes it, and a word says nothing of the volume. So the control plane could
  start a person's workspace on a disk it chose, whose code then runs as that workspace: it logs in
  as nobody, and pushes and calls through the egress proxy as the owner.
- **It can open every connected person's forge tokens.** The control plane holds the access and
  refresh tokens sealed under its own key, and with them could act on the forge directly, as each person,
  within the app's permissions (contents and pull requests, read and write) and the repositories
  that person reaches where the app is installed. Nothing on a host stands in the way, and the app
  installed on selected repositories and the forge's branch rules are the only limit. A refresh
  token it copied can outlive it until the person's authorization ends.
- **It can open every person's agent CLI credentials.** Their Claude Code and Codex tokens are
  sealed under its key (`agent_credentials`), as the forge's are, and with them it could use each
  person's provider account directly, until the person logs out or revokes them at the provider.
- **Machines the control plane's role starts.** Auto Scaling asks that role for `ec2:RunInstances`
  on the runners' launch template, and under that grant a call that names the template and other
  user data starts the machine with the other user data, tried on AWS on 2026-11-04; holding the
  instance to `ec2:IsLaunchTemplateResource` did not stop it. User data is not measured, so such a
  machine might attest as a runner under a document the control plane chose; whether it does has
  not been tried. It is told, not stopped: a rule emails `security_emails` within minutes of the
  call.
- **It can start a person's keyring anew.** It does through the account what a
  person who lost every key does (`StartKeyringAnew`), and a keyring started anew is somebody no
  access or roster signed before names - so it gets into none of their workspaces and none of their
  teams of more than one - but it can make new workspaces that answer to it, and sign the person's
  own team of one again (`roster.Roster.Start`), whose identity then names those workspaces. The CLI
  and the terminal show a keyring started anew before it is signed; nothing tells a person their
  account was used to start one.
- **A control plane can withhold the owner's newest access.** It carries every one, so before an
  access reaches the bucket it can keep it from the bucket and the host - a guest taken out
  logs in until the host reads it - and answer the owner's client with an older one. An access the
  bucket has is past withholding: the host reads it at every login, and takes no lower counter over
  it. A client builds the next access on what the control plane answers and keeps no record of its
  own, so over an access withheld before it reached the bucket it signs the guests it is shown -
  which the CLI prints and the terminal lists before anything is signed.
- **It can hand a host settings its owner signed before.** The host is handed the owner's
  settings as the control plane keeps them, and holds them to the owner's keyring, not to being the
  newest the owner signed: older settings, signed with a key the keyring still holds, are applied as
  readily. It also says whether a workspace is its owner's alone, which withholds their own
  settings where it says no and nothing where it says yes, and which prebuild a disk came from,
  whose claim the host still holds the checkout to.
- **I21 holds against a confused deputy, not this.** The control plane tags the
  session, so other code in it could tag it with any team, and it holds every value it reads in the
  clear, as it does a sealed one. The tag is only as good as who may tag a secret: a principal of
  the account that can tag one `spin-team-id` hands it to that team.
  Its role takes the control plane's credentials from anywhere while they last, so a reference is
  read off the machine where a sealed value is not: that needs the attested key.
- **The domain an identity is named under is the control plane's word.** It comes with the host's
  policy, and it can change it - which a relying party refuses, since the
  issuer it names publishes another key set: denial, not a widening. Who an identity is given for is
  the installation's list of audiences alone, which the control plane writes. A member of a parent team is no member of a team below it: a roster names a team's own
  members.
